endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: When implementing feedback activities, organizations should follow human subjects research requirements and best practices such as informed consent and subject compensation.

endorsements.title: Recommendations for the use of pediatric data in artificial intelligence and machine learning ACCEPT-AI
endorsements.quote: Because CYP cannot legally consent for themselves, federal regulations include special protections for pediatric study subjects, including parental consent and assent of older pediatric subjects.

endorsements.title: Promising for patients or deeply disturbing? The ethical and legal aspects of deepfake therapy
endorsements.quote: Clinical evaluation studies should be subject to ethical and legal review that considers the potential harms to participants as well as the interests of those depicted by deepfake technology, both of which we explored in this paper.

endorsements.title: Ethical oversight of AI-driven paediatric trials: a proactive, risk-sensitive interim review model
endorsements.quote: IRBs should develop systematic re-consent procedures when interim reviews identify consent documentation errors or when protocols materially change, requiring investigators to re-contact affected participants and audit completion rates.

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether applying human subjects protections to AI evaluation or feedback activities reduces exploitation or consent failures, and no supplied study documents how often the hazard occurs. The recommendation rests on one federal framework and two commentaries, all phrased as "should."

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. The three endorsements consist of one framework and two commentaries, which represent expert opinion. Under GRADE conventions, certainty about the practice's effect cannot be rated because no comparative or observational data exist.

NIST AI 600-1 advises that organizations follow human subjects research requirements, including informed consent and compensation, when running feedback activities. One commentary calls for ethical and legal review of deepfake therapy evaluations, and another asks IRBs to build re-consent procedures for paediatric AI trials. These sources express norms and do not report whether compliance changes outcomes.

No supplied study examined consent, compensation, or withdrawal in AI evaluation among Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. The paediatric commentary concerns minors, a group that depends on proxy consent, but it presents a review model rather than data on how such participants fare.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that measure how often people who take part in AI evaluation or feedback activities, such as clinicians rating outputs or patients testing chatbots, receive informed consent, compensation, and a clear withdrawal route. Such studies could then compare IRB-reviewed and non-reviewed activities on comprehension of consent, withdrawal rates, and reported harms.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. Organizations therefore have no data on whether standard consent and compensation procedures reach these groups as intended, which may matter most where consent forms rely on English reading ability.
